name: Wang Nan
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Women's World Cup singles title in 1997 at age 18 and reached the World Championships singles final the same year, becoming the successor to Deng Yaping as China's leading female table tennis player.
early_history_summary: Began playing table tennis at age seven in Fushun, Liaoning. Joined the Liaoning provincial team in 1992 and the Chinese national team in 1995. Won her first international singles title at the Scandinavian Open in 1994 at age 15, then won the Women's World Cup in 1997 and 1998.
family_context_summary: Born to a Chinese household in Fushun, Liaoning, with no prior athletic background in the family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: national team pipeline, early specialization, elite coaching, competitive peer environment
evidence_summary: Wang Nan began playing table tennis at age seven in Fushun and entered the Chinese national team pipeline at 16, benefiting from the world's most elite table tennis development system. She won her first international title at 15 and the World Cup at 18, succeeding Deng Yaping as China's leading player. Her family had no athletic background, but the national team infrastructure provided elite coaching, training partners, and international competition access from a young age.
starting_point: Born to a working-class Chinese household in Fushun, Liaoning, with no family athletic background.
current_position: Retired from competitive table tennis after the 2008 Beijing Olympics; inducted into the ITTF Hall of Fame; resides in China.

trajectory.event: Won her first international women's singles title at the Scandinavian Open.
Won the Women's World Cup singles title and reached the World Championships singles final in Manchester.
Became world number one in the ITTF rankings and won the World Championships singles title in Eindhoven.
Won Olympic gold medals in both singles and doubles at the Sydney Olympics.
Won World Championship titles in singles, doubles, and mixed doubles in Paris.
Won Olympic gold in doubles at the Athens Olympics.
Won Olympic team silver at the Beijing Olympics and retired from competitive play.

name: Vyacheslav Ivanov
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold in single sculls at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics at age 18, becoming the youngest Olympic champion in the event and the first Soviet rower to win single sculls gold.
early_history_summary: Started as a boxer in 1950, switched to rowing in 1952-53 at age 15. By 1955 at age 17, won the USSR junior championships and finished third in the senior championships, beating Olympic champion Yuriy Tyukalov. Won his first Soviet and European titles and Olympic gold in 1956 at age 18.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond being born in Moscow, USSR.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet sports system, early physical talent, dedicated coaching
evidence_summary: Ivanov started rowing at age 15 in Moscow and within three years won Olympic gold in single sculls at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics at age 18, benefiting from the Soviet Union's state-sponsored sports development system. He was coached by Demyanov and Nikolayev at CSKA Moscow. His rapid rise from beginner to Olympic champion suggests exceptional physical talent, though family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Moscow, USSR in 1938; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on August 5, 2024 at age 86 in Moscow; remembered as the first three-time consecutive Olympic gold medalist in single sculls.

trajectory.event: Won the USSR junior championships and finished third in the senior championships, beating Olympic champion Yuriy Tyukalov.
Won Olympic gold in single sculls at the Melbourne Olympics and European Championship gold.
Won second consecutive Olympic gold in single sculls at the Rome Olympics.
Won the first-ever World Championship gold in single sculls at Lucerne.
Won third consecutive Olympic gold in single sculls at the Tokyo Olympics.
Died on August 5, 2024 in Moscow.

name: Alfred Schnittke
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Schnittke was still a student at the Moscow Conservatory through 1961, completing his graduate work in composition at age 26-27. His Symphony No. 0 (1956) was a student work, and his first film scores and teaching appointment began in 1961-62, just after age 26.
early_history_summary: Began musical education in Vienna (1946-48) where his father was posted as a journalist, then moved to Moscow in 1948 and enrolled at the Moscow Conservatory in 1953, studying composition with Golubev. Composed a symphony in 1956 (later numbered No. 0) and completed graduate work in 1961.
family_context_summary: Father was a Jewish journalist and translator born in Frankfurt who moved to the Soviet Union in 1927; mother was a Volga German born in Russia. Paternal grandmother was a philologist and editor of German-language literature.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a journalist/translator; paternal grandmother was a philologist. No direct musical family background, but father's posting to Vienna gave Schnittke early exposure to Western classical music.

name: Walter Godefroot
milestone_by_age_26: Won bronze in the individual road race at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics at age 21, then turned professional and won the Belgian national road race championship in 1965, Liege-Bastogne-Liege in 1967, and the Tour of Flanders in 1968.
early_history_summary: Grew up in Ghent, Belgium, a cycling heartland. Won Olympic bronze in the road race at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics at age 21, then turned professional in 1965 with Wiel's-Groene Leeuw, immediately winning the Belgian national championship ahead of Eddy Merckx.
family_context_summary: Born in Ghent, German-occupied Belgium; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Flanders cycling culture, geographic immersion, competitive peer environment
evidence_summary: Godefroot grew up in Ghent, Belgium, in the heartland of Flemish cycling culture, which provided natural immersion in the sport from a young age. He won Olympic bronze in the road race at 21 in 1964 and turned professional the following year, immediately winning the Belgian national championship. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources, but the Belgian cycling ecosystem provided deep domain proximity and competitive peers including Eddy Merckx.
starting_point: Born in Ghent, German-occupied Belgium in 1943; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on September 1, 2025 at age 82 in Deurle, Belgium; final role was cycling team manager (Astana, 2007).

trajectory.event: Won bronze medal in the individual road race at the Tokyo Olympics.
Turned professional and won the Belgian national road race championship.
Won Liege-Bastogne-Liege, his first Monument classic.
Won the Tour of Flanders and Gent-Wevelgem.
Won Paris-Roubaix, beating rival Eddy Merckx by nearly three minutes.
Won the Tour de France points classification and a Giro d'Italia stage.
Won the first-ever Tour de France stage finishing on the Champs-Elysees.
Died on September 1, 2025 in Deurle, Belgium.

name: Gennady Golovkin
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold at the World Junior Boxing Championships in 2000 at age 18, followed by Asian Games gold in 2002 and World Amateur Championships gold in 2003, establishing himself as one of the world's top amateur middleweights before turning professional.
early_history_summary: Started boxing at age eight with his twin brother Max in Karaganda, Kazakhstan. Won the World Junior Championships in 2000 at age 18, Asian Games gold in 2002, and World Amateur Championships gold in 2003 at age 21, defeating future world champions including Matt Korobov and Andy Lee. Won Olympic silver in 2004 at age 22.
family_context_summary: Born to a Russian coal miner father and ethnic Korean mother who worked as a chemical laboratory assistant in Karaganda, Kazakh SSR. Two older brothers died in military service. Family had no boxing background.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were a coal miner and lab assistant with no known boxing connection.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early boxing start, massive amateur reps, Kazakh boxing pipeline, adversity catalyst
evidence_summary: Golovkin started boxing at age eight in Karaganda, Kazakhstan, with his twin brother, accumulating an estimated 350-plus amateur fights through the Soviet-style boxing development system. He won World Junior Championships gold at 18 and World Amateur Championships gold at 21. His father was a coal miner and mother a lab assistant; two older brothers died in military service, creating significant adversity. His first coach facilitated constant competition across gyms in his city, building exceptional early reps.
starting_point: Born to a Russian coal miner father and ethnic Korean mother who worked as a lab assistant in Karaganda, Kazakh SSR; family lived in poverty in post-Soviet Kazakhstan.
current_position: Former unified middleweight world champion; appointed President of the National Olympic Committee of Kazakhstan in 2024 and President of World Boxing in 2025; inducted into International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2026.

trajectory.event: Won gold medal at the World Junior Boxing Championships in Budapest.
Won gold medal at the Asian Games in Busan in the light middleweight division.
Won gold medal at the World Amateur Boxing Championships in Bangkok, defeating Matt Korobov and Andy Lee among others.
Won silver medal at the Athens Olympics in the middleweight division.
Won the WBA middleweight world title, beginning his professional championship reign.
Unified the WBA, WBC, and IBF middleweight titles by defeating David Lemieux.
Challenged Canelo Alvarez for the undisputed super middleweight championship in their trilogy fight.
Appointed President of World Boxing after playing a key role in maintaining Olympic boxing.

name: Toni Kukoč
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold at the FIBA U-18 European Championship in 1986 (MVP) and U-16 European Championship in 1985, then led Jugoplastika to three consecutive EuroLeague titles (1989-1991) and won Olympic silver with Yugoslavia in 1988, all before age 26.
early_history_summary: Grew up in Split, Croatia, and developed his game at Jugoplastika, the local club. Won U-16 and U-18 European championship golds with Yugoslavia in 1985-1986, was U-18 MVP in 1986 and U-19 World Championship MVP in 1987. Made senior EuroBasket debut in 1987, winning bronze, then led Jugoplastika to three EuroLeague titles from 1989-1991.
family_context_summary: Born in Split, SR Croatia, SFR Yugoslavia; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Jugoplastika youth system, Yugoslav basketball pipeline, early professional play, physical tools
evidence_summary: Kukoč grew up in Split, Croatia, and developed through the Jugoplastika basketball club system, one of Europe's premier academies. He won U-16 and U-18 European championship golds by age 17-18 and was playing professionally for Jugoplastika from age 16-17. His unique 6-foot-11 frame with point guard skills made him a transformative player. Family background is not documented, but the Jugoplastika and Yugoslav national team pipeline provided elite coaching, competition, and teammates from a young age.
starting_point: Born in Split, SR Croatia, SFR Yugoslavia in 1968; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Serves as special advisor to Jerry Reinsdorf, owner of the Chicago Bulls; inducted into Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame and FIBA Hall of Fame.

trajectory.event: Won gold at the FIBA U-16 European Championship with Yugoslavia and began playing for Jugoplastika.
Won gold and MVP at the FIBA U-18 European Championship.
Won MVP at the FIBA U-19 World Championship and made senior EuroBasket debut, winning bronze.
Won Olympic silver with Yugoslavia at the Seoul Olympics.
Led Jugoplastika to the first of three consecutive EuroLeague championships.
Won FIBA World Championship gold with Yugoslavia, named MVP; won second EuroLeague title with Jugoplastika.
Joined the Chicago Bulls in the NBA after playing for Benetton Treviso.
Won NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award and first NBA championship with the Chicago Bulls.

name: Terry Gou
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Gou founded Hon Hai Precision Industry (Foxconn) in 1974 at age 23-24 with a $7,500 loan, but the company was a small shed operation making plastic TV parts. Material success came later with the Atari deal in 1980 and China expansion in 1988.
early_history_summary: Born in Banqiao, Taiwan to parents who fled mainland China during the Chinese Civil War. Father was a policeman. Graduated from Taipei University of Marine Technology and worked in rubber and grinding wheel factories before founding Hon Hai Precision Industry in 1974 with $7,500 borrowed from his mother.
family_context_summary: Born to parents who fled mainland China's Shanxi Province to Taiwan in 1949. Father was a policeman who fought for the Kuomintang during the Chinese Civil War. Mother provided the $7,500 loan to start Foxconn.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a policeman; no family business or electronics background documented. Mother provided startup capital.

name: Aurelio Galfetti
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Galfetti studied architecture at ETH Zurich from 1954 to 1960 and opened his own office in Lugano in 1960 at age 24, completing his first building (Rotalinti house) in 1960-61. His major works came much later, starting with the Bellinzona swimming pool in 1967-70.
early_history_summary: Born in Biasca, Ticino, Switzerland. Studied architecture at ETH Zurich from 1954 to 1960, then opened his own architect's office in Lugano in 1960. His first built work was a single-family dwelling in Bellinzona (1960-61), but his major architectural works came in the late 1960s and 1970s.
family_context_summary: Born in Biasca, Ticino, Switzerland; family background not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Toni Sailer
milestone_by_age_26: Won all three alpine skiing gold medals (downhill, slalom, giant slalom) at the 1956 Winter Olympics at age 20, becoming the first to sweep all three events and the most successful athlete of the Games.
early_history_summary: Born and raised in Kitzbuhel, Tyrol, Austria, a world-renowned skiing center. A phenomenon as a teenager, won the downhill and combined at the Grand Prix at Megeve in 1952 at age 16. Suffered a broken leg in 1953 but returned to win his first Lauberhorn downhill in 1955 at age 19 before his historic Olympic triple crown in 1956.
family_context_summary: Born and raised in Kitzbuhel, Tyrol, Austria; father was a tinsmith. Family background otherwise not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a tinsmith; no documented family skiing background, though growing up in Kitzbuhel provided natural immersion in the sport.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Kitzbuhel skiing culture, elite ski club, geographic immersion, prodigy talent, competitive peers
evidence_summary: Sailer was born and raised in Kitzbuhel, Austria, one of the world's premier alpine skiing centers, and joined the Kitzbuhel Ski Club, providing unparalleled geographic and institutional immersion in the sport. He was a prodigy, winning the Grand Prix at Megeve at 16 and sweeping all three Olympic alpine golds at 20. His father was a tinsmith, but growing up in Kitzbuhel gave him natural access to world-class terrain, coaching, and competitive peers from childhood.
starting_point: Born in Kitzbuhel, Tyrol, Austria in 1935; father was a tinsmith. Grew up in one of the world's premier alpine skiing towns.
current_position: Died on August 24, 2009 at age 73 in Innsbruck, Austria; final roles included technical director of the Austrian national Alpine team (from 1972) and hotelier.

trajectory.event: Won the downhill and combined at the Grand Prix at Megeve, establishing himself as a teenage phenomenon.
Won his first Lauberhorn downhill at Wengen with a huge margin, signaling return to championship form after a broken leg in 1953.
Won all three alpine skiing gold medals (downhill, slalom, giant slalom) at the Cortina d'Ampezzo Winter Olympics.
Won two golds and a silver at the FIS World Championships in Bad Gastein, Austria.
Retired from competitive skiing to become a hotelier and film actor.
Appointed technical director of the Austrian national Alpine ski team.
Died on August 24, 2009 in Innsbruck after a long illness.

name: Gaston Roelants
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 3000m steeplechase gold at the 1962 European Championships at age 25 and won the International Cross Country Championships the same year, establishing himself as the world's top steeplechaser.
early_history_summary: Grew up in Opvelp, Belgium, the son of a farmer near Leuven. Started running at age 17 after his father forbade cycling. Made his international debut at the 1960 Olympics, finishing fourth in the steeplechase, then won European Championship gold and the International Cross Country title in 1962.
family_context_summary: Son of a farmer near Leuven, Belgium; father disapproved of sports and forbade cycling, leading Gaston to take up running secretly.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a farmer; no family athletic background documented. Father actively disapproved of sports.
primary_early_advantage_tags: late start, father's disapproval, self-driven training, exceptional physical capacity
evidence_summary: Roelants grew up on a farm near Leuven, Belgium, and started running at age 17 after his father forbade cycling. He trained secretly without parental support, developing an exceptional cardiovascular system through self-driven long hours in the forest. He made his Olympic debut at 23 in 1960, then won European Championship gold and the International Cross Country title at 25 in 1962. His late start and lack of family support make his rise a case of constraint-driven self-creation.
starting_point: Born in Opvelp, Belgium in 1937; son of a farmer near Leuven who disapproved of sports.
current_position: Retired former elite steeplechaser and cross country runner; living in Belgium at age 89.

trajectory.event: Made international debut at the Rome Olympics, finishing fourth in the 3000m steeplechase.
Won European Championship gold in the 3000m steeplechase and the International Cross Country Championships title.
Set his first world record in the 3000m steeplechase, clocking 8:29.6 in Leuven.
Won Olympic gold in the 3000m steeplechase at the Tokyo Olympics.
Set a second steeplechase world record of 8:26.4 in Leuven.
Improved his world records for 20km and the 1-hour race, and won his fourth International Cross Country title.
Retired from elite competition, continuing to race into his 40s and win masters world titles.

name: Isabel Allende
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Allende worked as a journalist and UN employee in the 1960s but did not publish her first novel until 1982 at age 40, when The House of the Spirits became a worldwide bestseller.
early_history_summary: Born in Lima, Peru to a Chilean diplomat father and mother who divorced when Allende was two. Grew up in Chile with grandparents, then moved with her mother and diplomat stepfather to Bolivia, Europe, and the Middle East. Worked as a journalist in Chile in the 1960s-70s and for the UN Food and Agriculture Organization before fleeing to Venezuela after the 1973 Pinochet coup.
family_context_summary: Daughter of Chilean diplomat Tomas Allende, first cousin of Salvador Allende (President of Chile 1970-73). Parents divorced when she was two; mother remarried diplomat Ramon Huidobro. Grew up in affluent but cash-constrained grandfather's household in Chile.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a diplomat; stepfather was a diplomat; uncle Salvador Allende was President of Chile. Family had political and diplomatic connections but no literary publishing background.

name: Ronnie James Dio
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Dio played in local and regional bands (The Vegas Kings, Ronnie and the Redcaps, Ronnie Dio and the Prophets) through the 1960s, releasing singles but achieving no significant commercial success. His fame arrived at age 33 when he joined Rainbow in 1975, and further with Black Sabbath in 1979.
early_history_summary: Born Ronald James Padavona in Portsmouth, New Hampshire to Italian-American parents. Started music career in 1957 at age 15 with The Vegas Kings, playing bass and vocals. Band evolved through several name changes to Ronnie Dio and the Prophets (1962-1967), releasing singles and one album. Formed Elf in 1967, which released three albums but did not achieve major commercial success.
family_context_summary: Born to Italian-American parents Patrick and Anna Padavona in Portsmouth, New Hampshire; family moved back to Cortland, New York. Father served in the U.S. Army during World War II. Family background otherwise not documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no known family musical background.
